common_name: Tetragona Aurea Hinoki Cypress (Golden Four-Angled Falsecypress)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, evenly moist soil where the four-angled golden sprays get enough sun to color well but some relief from the harshest midday exposure.

directions: Tetragona Aurea is an old, slow-growing Hinoki cypress selection named for its unusual four-sided, cord-like branchlets that give the foliage a twisted, almost braided texture rather than the flat sprays typical of the species. New growth emerges bright gold and holds color best with morning sun and afternoon shade in hot climates, fading toward yellow-green in deeper shade. Grow in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil and shelter from drying winter wind, which can brown exposed foliage; established plants otherwise need little more than an occasional check for interior deadwood. Its irregular, upright-conical habit and decades-long slow growth make it a specimen choice for conifer collections rather than a foundation plant needing quick fill-in.

common_name: Carsten's Wintergold Mugo Pine (Winter-Gold Dwarf Mountain Pine)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, siting where the winter foliage color will be visible from the house or a main path.

directions: Carsten's Wintergold is a true-dwarf mugo pine grown for its seasonal color shift: needles stay green through the growing season, then turn a striking bright gold through fall and winter before greening back up in spring. It forms a dense, low mound of short needles on tightly packed branches, growing only a couple of inches a year and staying compact for many seasons without shearing. Give it full sun and lean, sharply drained soil, since rich soil or shade both soften the winter gold color and encourage looser, less tidy growth. Once established it tolerates drought, wind, and poor soil, making it a reliable accent for rock gardens and winter-interest borders.

common_name: Valley Cushion Mugo Pine (Extreme Dwarf Cushion Pine)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; a raised bed or rock garden pocket suits its tiny mature footprint best.

directions: Valley Cushion is one of the most diminutive named mugo pine selections, originating as a witch's-broom find and growing into a flat, dense cushion of short dark-green needles that adds only a fraction of an inch a year. Its extreme dwarf habit and tight bun shape suit trough gardens, alpine beds, and miniature conifer collections where a full-size mugo pine would quickly overwhelm the space. Grow in full sun and lean, well-drained soil, since soggy roots or heavy shade cause it to open up and lose its dense form. It needs essentially no pruning or feeding, just protection from standing winter wet.

common_name: Cole's Prostrate Hemlock (Weeping Groundcover Canadian Hemlock)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade, ideally on a slope or wall top where the trailing branches can cascade.

directions: Cole's Prostrate hugs the ground so closely that it grows almost flat, sending stiff, ground-hugging branches outward in a tangled mat rather than mounding upward like most dwarf hemlocks. Draped over a rock or retaining wall, its branches cascade downward, making it one of the most useful true groundcover conifers for a shaded slope or the top of a dry-stacked wall. Keep the root zone consistently moist and shaded from hot afternoon sun, since hemlocks stress quickly in drought, and check periodically for hemlock woolly adelgid where that pest occurs. It needs no shearing to keep its flattened form, only occasional removal of any wayward upright shoot.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade, allowing plenty of horizontal room for the wide, mounded, weeping habit.

directions: Sargent's Weeping Hemlock is a classic, long-cultivated selection with no dominant central leader, instead building a broad, irregular mound of overlapping, cascading branches draped in fine, dark green needles. Left untrained it stays wider than tall for decades, forming one of the most graceful specimen conifers for a lawn or courtyard where its full spreading silhouette can be appreciated; it can also be staked while young to create a taller weeping form. Site it in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil with shelter from full afternoon sun and drying wind, and monitor for hemlock woolly adelgid in areas where the pest is established. Minimal pruning is needed beyond removing dead interior wood, since shearing disrupts its naturally irregular cascading outline.

common_name: Gentsch White Hemlock (Dwarf Cream-Tipped Canadian Hemlock)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade, where the cream-tipped new growth will show up best against darker foliage nearby.

directions: Gentsch White is a dwarf, dense-growing hemlock whose new spring growth emerges creamy white to pale yellow before settling into soft green, creating a two-toned, frosted look each flush that repeats through the growing season. Its slow, compact mounding habit and fine texture make it a good choice for shaded rock gardens and mixed dwarf conifer beds where a splash of pale color is welcome without a large mature footprint. Grow in evenly moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil with protection from hot afternoon sun and drying wind, and watch for hemlock woolly adelgid in affected regions. It tolerates light shaping if a tighter form is wanted but generally holds its shape well on its own.

common_name: Montgomery Dwarf Blue Spruce (Compact Globe Colorado Spruce)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to keep the steel-blue needle color dense and even.

directions: Montgomery is a long-popular dwarf selection of Colorado blue spruce that grows as a dense, broadly rounded to somewhat flat-topped mound of stiff, intensely silver-blue needles. It grows only a few inches a year, holding a tidy globe form for many years before slowly developing a more irregular, pyramidal outline with age, and rarely needs pruning to stay in scale with a foundation planting or rock garden. Full sun keeps the blue coloring at its most vivid, while shade or crowding leads to sparse, greener growth; average, well-drained soil is otherwise all it asks for. Water during establishment and dry spells, since spruce roots are shallow and can suffer in prolonged drought despite the plant's overall hardiness.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained soil where morning sun reaches the gold foliage but harsh afternoon exposure is buffered, especially in warmer parts of its range.

directions: Skylands is a slow-growing, narrowly pyramidal selection of Oriental spruce prized for its bright golden-yellow needles, among the most consistently vivid gold conifers sold for landscape use, holding color through most of the year rather than fading quickly to green. New growth is especially bright in spring, and the short, dense needles give the tree a fine, refined texture compared to bulkier gold conifers. It performs best with some afternoon shade or shelter in hot-summer climates to prevent needle scorch, paired with moist, well-drained soil and protection from strong winter wind. Growth is slow enough that it functions as a specimen accent for years before needing significant space, and pruning is rarely required beyond removing dead wood.

common_name: Pumila Norway Spruce (Dwarf Flat-Topped Mounding Spruce)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, allowing room to spread wider than it grows tall.

directions: Pumila is an old, well-established dwarf Norway spruce selection that builds a dense, flat-topped mound noticeably wider than it is tall, with short, dark green needles held on tightly packed branches. Its low, spreading habit and very slow annual growth make it a dependable anchor for dwarf conifer collections and foundation plantings where a tall spruce would quickly overwhelm the space. It tolerates full sun or light shade and adapts to a range of well-drained soils, needing little more than occasional water during extended dry spells once established. Left unpruned it keeps a naturally tidy cushion shape for decades, though an occasional errant shoot can be trimmed to preserve symmetry.

common_name: Sungold Sawara Cypress (Fine Golden Threadleaf Falsecypress)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, where the fine gold thread foliage can be seen up close.

directions: Sungold produces finer, more thread-like sprays than Golden Mop, giving the mounded shrub a softer, almost feathery texture in bright yellow-gold that holds its color well into fall. It grows slowly into a rounded, slightly irregular mound and stays in scale with foundation and rock garden plantings for many years without pruning. Full sun brings out the brightest gold tone, though a little afternoon shade in hot climates helps prevent tip burn; consistent moisture in well-drained soil keeps the fine foliage from browning in summer heat. Avoid heavy, poorly drained sites, which can lead to root and foliage disease in humid climates.

common_name: Tater Tot Arborvitae (Miniature Dense Globe Arborvitae)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; its tiny mature size suits containers, rock gardens, and tight border spots.

directions: Tater Tot is a newer, extremely compact globe arborvitae selection that grows into a dense, tightly rounded mound of soft green scale-like foliage, staying smaller at maturity than older miniature selections like Hetz Midget. Its slow, uniform growth needs essentially no shearing to maintain its naturally neat globe shape, making it useful for small-space landscaping, edging, and container culture where full-size arborvitae would be impractical. Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, and water regularly the first year or two while roots establish. Winter sun and wind can bronze the foliage slightly in exposed sites, but color typically greens back up with the return of warmer weather.
